title: Bhaichung Bhutia Urges Fans to Boycott India-Brazil Friendly as Pitch Concerns Mount
excerpt: India's football icon questions the ₹50-70 crore cost of hosting Brazil in Kolkata while clubs struggle to survive, as Brazilian delegation flags grass quality issues at Salt Lake Stadium.
body:
• Former India captain Bhaichung Bhutia has called on fans to boycott the October 3 friendly against Brazil at Kolkata's Salt Lake Stadium, questioning the reported ₹50-70 crore expenditure.
  • A five-member Brazilian Football Confederation delegation inspected the stadium and raised concerns about the grass density on both the main pitch and practice ground.
  • India withdrew from the inaugural FIFA ASEAN Cup to prioritise the Brazil fixture, a decision that has drawn sharp criticism from multiple quarters.
  • The AIFF may also arrange a friendly against Cape Verde around the same October window.

Bhaichung Bhutia, India's most decorated footballer, has called on fans to stay away from the upcoming friendly against Brazil, arguing that the reported ₹50-70 crore cost of staging the match represents a fundamental misallocation of resources at a time when Indian club football is in financial crisis.

'Boycott That Brazil Match'

Speaking on the 420 Grams podcast, Bhutia did not mince words. "Boycott that Brazil match. Then I think that is a big message. Then every organiser, every federation will think twice," he said.

The former captain's objection centres on the financial arithmetic. The All India Football Federation has planned to pay an advance to the Brazilian Football Confederation, with costs expected to be recovered through sponsors and private partners. Bhutia argues the money would deliver far greater returns if invested in grassroots development.

"If Rs 50 to 70 crore for one 90-minute match is going to Brazil, then what are we getting in return? Maybe 90 minutes of entertainment."

— Bhaichung Bhutia, former India captain

He proposed that the West Bengal government, which is expected to contribute to the match's funding, should instead invest in developing athletes for the Commonwealth Games and building futsal infrastructure across the state. "With ₹30 crore, make 100 futsal grounds — seven-a-side futsal grounds in 100 different districts," he said.

Brazilian Delegation Raises Pitch Concerns

Meanwhile, preparations for the October 3 fixture hit a practical snag when a five-member delegation from the CBF inspected Salt Lake Stadium on Thursday. Led by Sérgio Dimas de Oliveira, General Supervisor of the Men's National Teams, the officials spent over two hours assessing the venue's facilities, security arrangements and playing surface.

The delegation expressed concern about the grass density on both the main pitch and the practice ground, which has deteriorated due to the Durand Cup matches being played at the venue throughout August. They requested improvements to the turf after the Durand Cup concludes on August 23 and indicated they may return for a follow-up inspection.

The Brazilian officials also requested a separate room for coaching staff, physiotherapists and kit managers, in addition to the players' dressing room — a logistical requirement that could necessitate providing two dressing rooms for the visiting team.

A Broader Crisis in Indian Football

Bhutia's criticism comes against a backdrop of structural turmoil. India withdrew from the inaugural FIFA ASEAN Cup — where it was drawn alongside Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore — to accommodate the Brazil fixture. Jamshedpur FC exited the ISL after Tata Steel pulled out. The 2025-26 ISL season ran in a truncated format after the FSDL commercial agreement expired.

The AIFF has pushed back against the criticism, calling the match "a mutually agreed international sporting opportunity" and warning it would pursue legal remedies against those who "knowingly publish false and defamatory statements."

For diaspora football fans, the match represents an unprecedented spectacle — India facing the five-time World Cup champions for the first time at senior level. But Bhutia's argument resonates with those who have watched Indian football's commercial foundations erode while the federation pursues headline-grabbing fixtures. The October 3 date at Salt Lake Stadium, if it survives the pitch concerns, will test whether fans share his view or fill the stands regardless.
